title: Montezuma County CO well depth and drilling cost
meta_description: Montezuma County wells have a 100 ft median depth and 10 gpm median yield. Learn what that means for drilling cost and water supply on your property.
h1: Water wells in Montezuma County, Colorado
intro_html:
Montezuma County has a long history of domestic and stock wells in mixed sedimentary and fractured-bedrock ground. With more than 2,000 permitted wells on record, there’s enough data to set realistic expectations for well depth, production, and cost before you make an offer on land or plan a new build.

Here’s how the county’s well records translate into actual drilling decisions and risks for a home or small acreage outside places like Cortez, Dolores, Mancos, Lewis, and Towaoc.

sections.heading: How deep wells run in Montezuma County
sections.html:
Across Montezuma County, the median well depth is about 100 feet, with the middle half of wells between 38 and 200 feet. Half the wells on record are under 100 feet, and another 36% fall between 100 and 300 feet, so many homeowners get water without going especially deep by Colorado standards.

There are still some outliers: about 10% of wells go 300 to 600 feet, and around 5% are deeper than 600 feet, with the deepest on record reaching 1,820 feet. That wide spread tells you depth is site-specific. A driller will look at nearby wells in the same geologic setting, but you should still budget with a safety margin in case you land in tighter fractured-bedrock zones.

sections.heading: Well yields and how much water you can expect
sections.html:
Yield data in Montezuma County are generally favorable. The median reported yield is 10 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells fall between 5 and 15 gpm. For a single home on an exempt domestic well, that’s usually more than enough for household use and some reasonable outdoor watering, as long as you stay within Colorado’s household-use and 35 gpm pumping limits.

The county still has some weaker producers: 4% of tested wells report under 1 gpm and 20% fall between 1 and 5 gpm. On the other end, 45% land in the 5 to 15 gpm range and 30% report 15 gpm or more. When you evaluate a parcel, pay close attention to nearby well yields; a low-gpm well can still work, but it may require storage and more careful water management.

sections.heading: Water table depth and recent trends
sections.html:
Static water levels in Montezuma County are moderate. The median depth to water is about 40 feet, with the middle half between 13 and 80 feet below ground surface. That means many wells hit water well above their total drilled depth, which helps with pumping costs and can make older, shallower completions viable.

Looking at trends, the median static level in the 2010s was 40 feet, and in the 2020s it is also 40 feet. Based on the countywide data, there’s no clear sign of a general drop in the water table over those decades. Conditions can still vary by ridge, valley, or mesa, so check individual well logs close to your specific tract for a more precise picture.

sections.heading: Who’s drilling here and permit history
sections.html:
Montezuma County’s well records go back decades. Only a handful of permits show up in the 1950s and 1960s, then activity picked up sharply: 130 permits in the 1970s, 293 in the 1980s, and 366 in the 1990s. The 2000s saw 308 permits, with 263 in the 2010s and 142 already in the 2020s, including permits as recent as 2025.

Most wells are for domestic or household use, at 66% of the total, with stock, irrigation, and a substantial number of monitoring wells making up the rest. Drilling has been carried out by several outfits over time, with significant numbers of wells attributed to Mcpherson Drilling Co. (Mcpherson, Billy G.), Authorized (Pe, Pg), and Ancell Drilling Service (Ancell, Lee). That long permit history gives you a solid pool of nearby examples to review before committing to a new well.

sections.heading: What a new well is likely to cost in Montezuma County
sections.html:
The county’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground typically drills in the range of about $50 to $75 per foot. At the 100-foot median depth, that translates to roughly $5,000 to $7,500 for the drilled hole alone. When you add casing, grout, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical work, a finished residential well often lands in the ballpark of $11,000 to $19,500.

Remember that depth can be highly variable, from 38 feet for some shallower wells up to several hundred feet or more. If your neighbors are in the 200-foot range, use that for budgeting instead of the countywide median. It’s smart to build contingency into your construction budget so a deeper-than-expected hole or a second attempt doesn’t derail the project.

sections.heading: Risks: water quality, low yield, and site layout
sections.html:
Most Montezuma County wells are completed in unnamed fractured-bedrock aquifers, with smaller numbers in formations like the Dakota and Mancos. Fractured rock brings natural variability in yield and sometimes mineral content. On top of that, there are mapped environmental concerns in the broader area: 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 11 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles.

Those don’t mean your specific well is contaminated, but they are a clear signal to test thoroughly, especially near industrial or historic mining areas. Given that 4% of tested wells make under 1 gpm, low yield is another real risk to plan for. Septic placement and setbacks from the well also matter on smaller parcels, so think through building footprints and drain fields early.

sections.heading: Buying or building on a lot in Montezuma County
sections.html:
Before you buy, pull the state well records for the nearest permits around your property in communities like Cortez, Dolores, Mancos, Lewis, or Towaoc. Compare their depths to the county median of 100 feet and see if your immediate area tends to run shallower or deeper, and what kind of yields they report relative to the 10 gpm countywide median.

Check how many of those nearby wells list static water levels and note where water is actually standing in the hole compared to ground surface. Because aquifers here are mostly fractured bedrock, one parcel can differ from the next, so don’t rely on a single good or bad well. Plan for full water-quality testing, review local environmental maps, and talk to a qualified driller about realistic depth and cost scenarios before you finalize plans.

faq.q: How deep are water wells in Montezuma County, Colorado?
faq.a: Based on state permit records, the median well depth in Montezuma County is about 100 feet. The middle half of wells fall between 38 and 200 feet. Around half of all wells are under 100 feet, and most of the rest are under 300 feet, but a small share reach 300 to 600 feet or even deeper, with one well on record at 1,820 feet.

faq.q: What is a typical well yield in Montezuma County?
faq.a: Reported yields in Montezuma County are generally solid for household use. The median yield is 10 gallons per minute, and the middle half of wells produce between 5 and 15 gpm. About 4% of wells report under 1 gpm and 20% fall between 1 and 5 gpm, while a large share are at 5 to 15 gpm or higher, which usually supports a home and modest outdoor use.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Montezuma County?
faq.a: In Montezuma County’s mixed sedimentary and alluvial ground, typical drilling runs about $50 to $75 per foot. At the county’s 100-foot median depth, that’s roughly $5,000 to $7,500 for the borehole itself. A complete residential well system, including casing, pump, pressure tank, trenching, and electrical, often totals in the range of about $11,000 to $19,500, depending on site and depth.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Montezuma County?
faq.a: Safety depends on the specific well. Most wells tap fractured-bedrock aquifers, with some in formations like the Dakota and Mancos. There are 24 PFAS sampling or contamination sites, 14 historic mine features, and 11 EPA Superfund or cleanup sites within about 10 miles, so water-quality testing is important. Have a lab test for bacteria, metals, and any site-specific contaminants before relying on a well for drinking.

faq.q: Are groundwater levels dropping in Montezuma County?
faq.a: Countywide records don’t show a clear recent decline. The median static water level was about 40 feet below ground in the 2010s and remains about 40 feet in the 2020s. Individual wells can behave differently based on local geology and pumping, so you should still review static-water data from nearby wells to see how your immediate area compares to the countywide trend.
